title: The Master and Margarita, Bulgakov
subject: litterature
description: The devil visits Stalin's Moscow while a writer tells the story of Pontius Pilate. Bulgakov's answer to censorship: manuscripts do not burn.

hero.hook: Satan in Moscow, Pilate in Jerusalem: the novel written in secret under Stalin.

blocks.text: **The Master and Margarita** was written between **1928** and **1940**, then published in **1967**. It weaves three worlds together: Soviet Moscow in the 1930s, ancient Jerusalem, and a fantastic realm ruled by the devil. **Mikhail Bulgakov**, who was born in **1891** and died in **1940**, planned it as an artistic testament written under the censorship of **Stalin**.

The book argues that the truth of art wins out in the end over political repression, even when the author has to write in complete secrecy. Its famous line “Manuscripts do not burn” has become a symbol of cultural resistance.

**Mikhail Bulgakov**, a doctor turned playwright, saw his plays banned from the late 1920s on. In **1930**, he asked the government either for permission to leave the country or for the right to work. **Stalin** found him a job at the theater, but his major works stayed locked away.

blocks.caption: Mikhail Bulgakov, a persecuted writer who dictated his novel on his deathbed

blocks.text: Afraid of a raid by the [[NKVD]], the Soviet political police and the ancestor of the KGB, Bulgakov burned the first manuscript in **1930**, then wrote it again from memory.

In **1940**, blind, he dictated the last corrections from his deathbed. The novel was not published in full until **1967**, twenty-seven years after his death, thanks to the stubbornness of his widow.

sections.title: A story built like a symphony

blocks.text: In **Moscow**, **Woland**, who is Satan, turns up with his black cat **Behemoth** and spreads panic through the corrupt literary caste. At the same time, the **Master** is writing the story of **Pontius Pilate** and **Yeshua Ha-Nozri** in Jerusalem. Yeshua is the name given to Jesus in that story. The two narratives answer each other.

blocks.caption: Moscow in the 1930s: the setting for Bulgakov's political satire

blocks.text: **Margarita** agrees to become a witch and to preside over the devil's ball, all to save the Master, shut in an asylum after his manuscript was destroyed. Her sacrifice out of love ties the ancient past to the Soviet present. Bulgakov braids three registers together: political satire, biblical story, and pure fantasy.

sections.title: The metaphysics of cowardice and evil

blocks.text: Bulgakov redefines the devil. Woland shows that human beings have not changed at all, whatever the promises of [[Socialist realism]]. That official Soviet doctrine required art to serve the party. **Cowardice** is “the most terrible of vices”, the vice of Pilate and of the Soviet critics who betray their colleagues.

blocks.attribution: Mikhail Bulgakov, The Master and Margarita

blocks.text: The line claims that true ideas outlive censorship. The Master is saved because his work is genuine, while his attackers sink into oblivion. Pilate, for his part, is condemned to wander forever for letting Yeshua be executed out of cowardice.

In the USSR the novel circulated as [[Samizdat]], secret typed copies of banned writing. People read it in low voices among friends. It brought the sacred and the fantastic back into a daily life smothered by official ideology.
The novel gave Mick Jagger the idea for “Sympathy for the Devil” after Marianne Faithfull handed him an English translation in **1967**.

Margarita, set free by love and magic, has become an icon of active devotion. Bulgakov mixes black humor and tragedy to ask where an individual stands against a totalitarian system. His novel remains one of the most subversive of the 20th century.
Bulgakov wrote this novel in secret to say that cowardice is the worst of sins and that genuine art always survives the flames.
